title: Natural Numbers (Natürliche Zahlen), Peano Axioms, and Induction
summary: This unit introduces the natural numbers and their characterization by the Peano axioms (Peano-Axiome). It covers the successor function (Nachfolgerfunktion), the induction axiom (Induktionsaxiom), recursive definitions (rekursive Definitionen), ordinary induction (Induktion), and strong induction (starke Induktion). Applications include prime factorization (Primfaktorzerlegung) and tilings of square boards with L-trominoes (L-Trominos).
keyFacts: The Peano axioms characterize $\mathbb{N}_0$ using a distinguished number $nil$ and a successor function $S$.
Axiom 3 requires $S(n)\neq nil$ for every $n$; no arrow may point to $nil$.
Axiom 4 requires the successor function to be injective: $S(m)=S(n)\Rightarrow m=n$.
The induction axiom rules out unreachable extra elements and is stated formally as $\mathbb{N}_0\subseteq X\iff 0\in X\wedge\forall n\in X\cap\mathbb{N}_0:n+1\in X$.
A recursive definition requires finitely many explicit initial values and a rule for the subsequent values.
An induction proof consists of an induction base and an induction step; the induction step uses the induction hypothesis for an arbitrary but fixed $n$.
For induction starting at $n_0$, the base case must start at $n_0$.
Strong induction allows all cases $P(k)$ with $n_0\le k\le n$ as the induction hypothesis.
Every natural number $n\ge2$ is a product of primes; strong induction establishes existence.
The uniqueness of prime factorization does not follow from strong induction alone.
A $2^n\times2^n$ board with one square removed can be tiled with L-trominoes.
In the induction step of the tromino proof, the board is divided into four quadrants, and a central tromino is placed in the three complete quadrants.
A $2^n\times2^n$ board with one square missing requires $(4^n-1)/3$ L-trominoes.

questions.prompt: Which statement is true of $\mathbb{N}_0$?

options.text: It is the set of all integers except zero.
It is the first infinite set.
It contains exactly the real numbers between 0 and 1.
It is a finite set with exactly zero elements.

questions.explanation: $\mathbb{N}_0$ is characterized as the first infinite set. The other descriptions do not apply to $\mathbb{N}_0$.

questions.prompt: Which Peano axiom describes the injectivity of the successor function?

options.text: There is a distinguished natural number $nil$.
All natural numbers are included along with $nil$ and every successor.
$S(m)=S(n)$ implies $m=n$.
For every $n$, $S(n)\neq nil$.

questions.explanation: Axiom 4 states $S(m)=S(n)\Rightarrow m=n$ and prevents two distinct numbers from having the same successor.

questions.prompt: The Peano axioms use a distinguished number `nil` and a successor function $S$. The third axiom states: For every natural number $n$, $S(n) \neq nil$. Claim: According to this axiom, `nil` cannot be the successor of a natural number. Is the claim true or false?

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The third Peano axiom states exactly that for every natural number $n$, its successor $S(n)$ is not `nil`. Thus no arrow can point to `nil`.

questions.prompt: The formal induction axiom is: $\mathbb{N}_0\subseteq X\iff ___$.

options.text: $0\in X\wedge\forall n\in X\cap\mathbb{N}_0:n+1\in X$
$X\subseteq\mathbb{N}_0\wedge\forall n\in X:n-1\in X$
$0\notin X\vee\forall n\in\mathbb{N}_0:n+1\notin X$
$1\in X\wedge\forall n\in X:n+2\in X$

questions.explanation: The set must contain $0$ and, whenever it contains a natural number $n$, it must also contain its successor $n+1$.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes tuples from words?

options.text: Tuples consist exclusively of characters from an alphabet.
Concatenation is always associative for tuples and never associative for words.
Nesting can matter for tuples, whereas concatenation of words is associative.
Words always have a fixed length, whereas tuples can have any length.

questions.explanation: For tuples, for example, $(a,(b,c))\neq((a,b),c)$. Concatenation of words is associative: $a(bc)=(ab)c$.

questions.prompt: Which representation is the MSBF binary representation of the number $6$?
questions.explanation: MSBF writes the most significant bit first. $6=4+2$ therefore gives $110$; $011$ would be the LSBF representation.

questions.prompt: Select all the true statements. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: The unary representation of $n$ uses $n$ strokes.
LSBF means that the most significant bit comes first.
In Gray code, consecutive numbers differ in exactly one bit.
In the von Neumann representation, $0=\emptyset$.
A word may consist only of arbitrary set-theoretic objects, not alphabet characters.

questions.explanation: Gray code, the von Neumann representation, and unary representation are defined this way. LSBF instead writes the least significant bit first; words consist of characters from an alphabet.

questions.prompt: What is an essential part of a recursive definition of a sequence?

options.text: A random selection of individual sequence terms.
Explicit initial values and a rule for obtaining later values from already defined ones.
Only the claim that a formula might exist.
Only a closed-form expression, without initial values.

questions.explanation: A recursive definition starts with finitely many explicit values and then computes each subsequent value from previously defined values.

questions.prompt: In the induction base, the induction hypothesis may be used to prove $P(0)$.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The induction base proves $P(0)$ without reference to $P(n)$. The induction hypothesis is used only in the induction step.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes the induction hypothesis for strong induction starting at $n_0$?

options.text: For every $k\ge n_0$, $P(k+1)$ already holds.
For every $k$ with $n_0\le k\le n$, $P(k)$ holds.
Only $P(n_0)$ holds.
Only $P(n+1)$ holds.

questions.explanation: In strong induction, all previous cases from $n_0$ through $n$ are assumed as the induction hypothesis.

questions.prompt:
What structure does this diagram represent?

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    nil((nil)) --> e1((S(nil))) --> e2((S(S(nil)))) --> d(("…"))
```

options.text: A finite cycle with three nodes.
A doubly infinite chain with no distinguished starting point.
A one-way infinite Peano chain with no return.
A chain in which two predecessors converge.

questions.explanation: The diagram shows the distinguished starting point $nil$, followed each time by a uniquely determined successor. There is neither a cycle nor a return to the start.

questions.prompt: For the recursively defined sequence $a_0=0$ and $a_n=2a_{n-1}+1$ for $n>0$, what is the value of $a_4$?
questions.explanation: Working step by step gives $a_1=1$, $a_2=3$, $a_3=7$, and $a_4=15$. At each step, evaluate the recurrence as $2a_{n-1}+1$.

questions.prompt: Which calculation correctly uses the induction hypothesis for $a_n=2^n-1$ in the induction step?

options.text: $a_{n+1}\overset{\mathrm{Def}}{=}2a_n+1\overset{\mathrm{IA}}{=}2(2^n-1)+1=2^{n+1}-1$

questions.explanation: First substitute the recursive definition, then use the IH $a_n=2^n-1$. The simplification gives exactly $2^{n+1}-1$.

questions.prompt: Evaluate using the geometric sum formula $\sum_{k=0}^{3}2^k$.
questions.explanation: The sum is $1+2+4+8=15$. The formula gives $(1-2^4)/(1-2)=15$ as well.

questions.prompt: The formula $\sum_{k=0}^{n}x^k=\frac{1-x^{n+1}}{1-x}$ can also be applied directly when $x=1$.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: For $x=1$, the denominator would be $1-x=0$. Therefore, the formula is stated explicitly only for $x\neq1$.

questions.prompt: At which starting value must induction for the statement $2^n>n^2$ begin if the statement is to hold continuously from that point onward?
questions.explanation: The statement is false for $n=2,3,4$ and holds again from $n=5$ onward. Therefore, the induction base must establish $P(5)$.

questions.prompt: For $a_0=0$ and $a_n=2a_{n-1}+1$ for $n>0$, select all the true statements. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: For every $n\in\mathbb{N}_0$, $a_n=2^n-1$.

questions.explanation: The sequence begins with $0,1,3,7$. The recurrence gives the statement for $a_{n+1}$, and the lecture proves the closed form $2^n-1$ by induction.

questions.prompt: An $8\times 8$ board is divided into four $4\times 4$ quadrants. One square in quadrant Q1, at the top left, is already missing. An L-tromino consists of three squares and is placed at the center of the board: it covers the innermost corner square of each of the other quadrants, Q2, Q3, and Q4. For the induction step, assume that every $4\times 4$ board with exactly one missing or already covered square can be tiled with L-trominoes. What follows from placing the central tromino?

context.content:
flowchart TD
  B["8×8-Brett: ein Feld fehlt in Q1"] --> Z["In vier 4×4-Quadranten teilen"]
  Z --> Q1["Q1 oben links: ursprüngliches Feld fehlt"]
  Z --> M["Mittel-L belegt je ein inneres Eckfeld in Q2, Q3 und Q4"]
  M --> Q2["Q2: ein Feld belegt"]
  M --> Q3["Q3: ein Feld belegt"]
  M --> Q4["Q4: ein Feld belegt"]
context.caption: The initial configuration and the effect of the central tromino on the four quadrants.

options.text: Each of the four quadrants now has exactly one missing or already covered square, so it satisfies the induction hypothesis.
Only Q1 now has a missing or covered square; Q2, Q3, and Q4 remain complete.
The entire $8\times 8$ board is treated as a single L-tromino.
The four quadrants are combined into a larger square.

questions.explanation: Q1 still contains the originally missing square. The central tromino covers one inner corner square in each of Q2, Q3, and Q4. Thus each $4\times 4$ quadrant has exactly one square that needs no further coverage and can be tiled using the stated induction hypothesis.

questions.prompt: A square board consists of $8 \times 8$ unit squares. Exactly one square has been removed. The remaining squares are covered completely, without overlap, by L-trominoes; each L-tromino covers exactly 3 squares. How many trominoes are needed?
questions.explanation: $8 \cdot 8 - 1 = 63$ squares remain. Each tromino covers 3 squares, so $63 / 3 = 21$ trominoes are needed.

questions.prompt: A 3-bit Gray-code sequence is fully specified here as `000 → 001 → 011 → 010 → 110 → 111 → 101 → 100` and then continues again from `000`. Which code comes immediately after `011` in this order?
questions.explanation: In the given sequence, `010` comes immediately after `011`.

questions.prompt: In the von Neumann representation, the successor is defined recursively by $n+1:=n\ ___\ \{n\}$.

options.text: $\cap$
$\times$
$\setminus$
$\cup$

questions.explanation: The definition is $n+1:=n\cup\{n\}$. Thus each number contains exactly its predecessors.

questions.prompt: An $8\times8$ board has one missing square. Select all the true statements. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Exactly $21$ L-trominoes are needed.
$63$ squares remain to be covered.
Each of the four quadrants has size $4\times4$.
The missing square lies in all four quadrants at once.
$20$ L-trominoes are needed because each tromino covers four squares.

questions.explanation: $8\times8$ has $64$ squares; after one is removed, $63=21\cdot3$ remain. Each of the four quadrants has size $4\times4$, and the missing square lies in exactly one of them.

questions.prompt: The induction step alone already proves that $P(n)$ holds for every $n\in\mathbb{N}_0$.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The induction step only describes how to pass from $P(n)$ to $P(n+1)$. Without a valid induction base, the chain does not get started.

questions.prompt: Why can a finite set with $k$ elements not satisfy Peano axioms 1–4?

options.text: Because the $k$ successors must have distinct targets by axiom 4, but axiom 3 allows only $k-1$ possible targets.
Because axiom 4 explicitly makes the successor function non-injective.
Because axiom 1 requires at least $k+1$ distinguished numbers.
Because axiom 3 requires $nil$ itself to be a successor.

questions.explanation: Axiom 3 rules out $nil$ as a target, leaving only $k-1$ possible targets. But axiom 4 requires $k$ distinct successor targets for the $k$ elements.

questions.prompt: Select all correct matches for the Peano axioms. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Axiom 2 prevents dead ends.
Axiom 5 explicitly allows unreachable extra elements.
Axiom 3 prevents arrows from pointing to $nil$.
Axiom 4 prevents two successor paths from merging.

questions.explanation: Axiom 2 requires every number to have a successor, axiom 3 forbids $nil$ as a successor, and axiom 4 enforces injectivity. Axiom 5 rules out unreachable extra elements.

questions.prompt:
Which Peano axiom fails for this candidate?

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    nil((nil)) --> hugo((hugo)) --> hugo
```

options.text: Axiom 4, because $S(nil)=S(hugo)$ even though $nil\neq hugo$.
Axiom 2, because $hugo$ has no successor.
Axiom 1, because $nil$ is missing.
Axiom 3, because an arrow points to $nil$.

questions.explanation: Here, $S(nil)=hugo$ and $S(hugo)=hugo$. Thus two distinct elements have the same successor, violating the injectivity required by axiom 4.

questions.prompt: Why is the assumption $x\neq1$ needed for the geometric sum formula?

options.text: Otherwise, the first summand $x^0$ would be undefined.
Because the sum exists only for negative $x$.
Otherwise, $x^{n+1}$ would always be zero.
Otherwise, the denominator $1-x$ is zero.

questions.explanation: For $x=1$, the denominator becomes $1-x=0$, so the stated fractional formula is not valid.

questions.prompt: Evaluate $\sum_{k=0}^{3} 2^k$ using the geometric sum formula $\sum_{k=0}^{n} x^k = (1 - x^{n+1})/(1 - x)$ for $x \neq 1$.

For every number $m \ge 2$, let $P(m)$ be the statement: “$m$ is a product of primes.” In an induction step, we want to prove $P(n+1)$, where $n \ge 2$. The strong induction hypothesis is: $P(k)$ holds for every $k$ with $2 \le k \le n$. If $n+1$ is composite, it can be written as $a \cdot b$ with $2 \le a,b \le n$. Which statements are true? Select all correct answers.

options.text: It is always enough to assume only $P(n)$, because every factor equals $n$.
Strong induction automatically proves the uniqueness of prime factorization as well.
In the composite case, the induction hypothesis can be applied to both factors $a$ and $b$.
The factors $a$ and $b$ are smaller factors of $n+1$ and need not equal $n$.
The induction hypothesis covers all $k$ with $2 \le k \le n$.

questions.explanation: The factors of a composite $n+1$ are smaller than $n+1$ and lie between 2 and $n$. The strong induction hypothesis covers both. This proof establishes the existence of a prime factorization; uniqueness requires a separate proof.

questions.prompt: What does strong induction directly establish in the proof of prime factorization?

options.text: The existence of a prime factorization.
That every prime number is even.
That every natural number is itself prime.
The uniqueness of the factorization up to order.

questions.explanation: The induction handles the prime case and the composite case, thereby establishing existence. Uniqueness requires an additional argument.

questions.prompt: Because $4^n-1$ is divisible by $3$, the tiling of any punctured $2^n\times2^n$ board has already been proved.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Divisibility is only a plausibility check. The actual proof requires dividing the board into four quadrants and using the central tromino.

questions.prompt:
Which statement correctly completes the induction step shown in the diagram?

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    B["Brett mit einem fehlenden Feld"] --> Q["In 4 Quadranten teilen"]
    Q --> M["Mittel-Tromino"]
    M --> Q1["Quadrant 1"]
    M --> Q2["Quadrant 2"]
    M --> Q3["Quadrant 3"]
    M --> Q4["Quadrant 4"]
```

options.text: Only the original quadrant satisfies the induction hypothesis.
The central tromino removes the original missing square.
After the central tromino is placed, exactly one square is missing from each quadrant, so the induction hypothesis applies four times.
The quadrants must be recombined into a $2^{n+1}\times2^{n+1}$ board.

questions.explanation: The original quadrant contains the actual missing square; the central tromino covers one corner square in each of the other three. Thus all four sub-boards have the same form as in the induction base.

questions.prompt: How should an induction for a statement “for every $n\ge n_0$” be started?

options.text: Without an induction base, provided the step is algebraically correct.
With $P(0)$ and an induction step starting at $n=0$.
With $P(n_0-1)$ and a step only for $n=n_0$.
With $P(n_0)$ and an induction step for arbitrary $n\ge n_0$.

questions.explanation: The range of validity begins at $n_0$. Therefore, the base must prove $P(n_0)$, and the step must go from an arbitrary $n\ge n_0$ to $n+1$.

questions.prompt: For the claim $2^n>n^2$ for every $n\in\mathbb{N}_0$, it already holds that at $n=2$: $4\not>4$. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: $n=2$ is a counterexample; the claim starting at $0$ is false, and a suitable induction must start later.
The counterexample shows only that the induction base must be at $n=1$.
The case $n=2$ is irrelevant to a universal statement.
The induction step automatically makes the false base harmless.

questions.explanation: A single counterexample disproves a universal statement. Here the statement must be restricted to a range starting at $n_0=5$ before induction is appropriate.

questions.prompt: Why does every finite candidate with $k$ elements already fail to satisfy Peano axioms 1–4?

options.text: Axiom 4 allows all successors to be equal.
Axiom 1 forbids every finite base set.
Axiom 3 requires every node to have two successors.
Axiom 2 produces $k$ successors, which must be distinct by axiom 4, but axiom 3 allows only $k-1$ possible targets.

questions.explanation: This is exactly a pigeonhole argument: $k$ distinct successor targets would have to fit into only $k-1$ allowed targets. Therefore, the chain cannot be finite.

questions.prompt: Which combination respects both the structure of tuples and that of words?

options.text: $(a,(b,c))\neq((a,b),c)$ and $a(bc)=(ab)c$
Both expressions are associative.
Neither expression is associative.
$(a,(b,c))=((a,b),c)$ and $a(bc)\neq(ab)c$

questions.explanation: Tuples retain their nesting, whereas word concatenation is associative. Thus the two equations in answer b are correct.

questions.prompt: For the sequence $a_0=0$ and $a_n=2a_{n-1}+1$, $P(n):a_n=2^n-1$ was proved by induction. What follows for $a_4$?
questions.explanation: The proved formula implies $a_4=2^4-1=16-1=15$. The recurrence gives the same value step by step.

questions.prompt: In the strong induction step for the existence of a prime factorization of $n+1$, the cases are analyzed. Select all the true statements. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: The induction hypothesis holds for every $k$ with $2\le k\le n$.
If $n+1$ is prime, the proof for this case is complete.
An induction hypothesis only for $P(n)$ suffices, regardless of $a$ and $b$.
Uniqueness up to order follows automatically from these two cases.
If $n+1=a\cdot b$ with $2\le a,b\le n$, the induction hypothesis may be applied to $a$ and $b$.

questions.explanation: The strong induction hypothesis covers all smaller numbers. Thus it works for both the prime case and the composite case; uniqueness is not proved automatically.

questions.prompt: A candidate consists of the genuine chain $nil\to1\to2\to\dots$ and a separate cycle $hugo\tootto\tohugo$. Which axiom rules out this candidate?

options.text: Axiom 5, because the reachable part does not contain the separate cycle.
Axiom 4, because two different successors merge in the cycle.
Axiom 1, because $nil$ is not distinguished.
Axiom 2, because the genuine chain has no successors.

questions.explanation: The set of elements reachable from $nil$ contains $nil$ and is closed under the successor function. Axiom 5 then requires it to contain all natural numbers, which is not true of the separate cycle.

questions.prompt: An $8 \times 8$ board has 64 unit squares. Exactly one square has been removed. How many L-trominoes, each covering exactly 3 squares, are needed to cover all the remaining squares completely and without overlap?
questions.explanation: $8^2 - 1 = 63$ squares remain. Each L-tromino covers 3 squares, so $63 / 3 = 21$ trominoes are required.

questions.prompt: In the induction step for the geometric sum, which transformation is the appropriate next step after separating off the last summand?

options.text: $\sum_{k=0}^{n+1}x^k=\sum_{k=0}^{n}x^k-x^{n+1}$, and then use the induction hypothesis.
Cancel the fraction by $1-x=0$.
$\sum_{k=0}^{n+1}x^k=\sum_{k=0}^{n}x^k+x^{n+1}$, and then use the induction hypothesis.
$\sum_{k=0}^{n+1}x^k=x^{n+1}$, because all earlier summands disappear.

questions.explanation: The standard trick is to separate off the last summand, substitute the induction hypothesis for the partial sum, and then simplify the fraction.

questions.prompt: Which components are needed for a correct induction proof of the geometric sum formula? Select all the true statements. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: The induction hypothesis alone proves the formula for every $n$, even without a base case.
The assumption $x\neq1$ prevents division by zero.
The induction step may be carried out only for $n=0$.
In the induction step, separate off the last summand and use the induction hypothesis.
The induction base checks the case $n=0$.

questions.explanation: The base case, a valid domain, and the algebraic step are all necessary. The induction hypothesis without a base is insufficient, and the step must hold for an arbitrary fixed $n$.

questions.prompt: In the tromino induction step, the originally missing square may lie in any of the four quadrants; after the central tromino is placed, each quadrant then has exactly one missing square.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The originally missing square lies in exactly one quadrant. The central tromino covers one corner square in each of the other three, so all four quadrants satisfy the induction hypothesis.

questions.prompt: An $2^5\times2^5$ board has one missing square. How many L-trominoes are needed according to Golomb's theorem?
questions.explanation: The board has $4^5=1024$ squares. After one is removed, $1023$ remain, and $1023/3=341$ L-trominoes are needed.

levels.title: Practice: Numbers, Codes, and Clever Tricks

questions.prompt: You read the position of a digital rotary encoder, such as one in a volume control. Its adjacent states are encoded so that exactly one bit changes. Which concept is behind this?

options.text: Gray code
Geometric sum
L-tromino tiling
Strong induction

questions.explanation: In Gray code, adjacent codewords differ in exactly one bit. This can reduce ambiguity when a rotary encoder moves between adjacent states.

questions.prompt: You are building a monthly spreadsheet in Excel: the account balance in month $n$ is calculated from the previous month's balance plus the new deposit. Which concept best describes this construction?

options.text: Pigeonhole principle
Gray code
Recursive definition
L-tromino tiling

questions.explanation: Each new value is generated from a value already determined. This is a recursive definition, for example $a_{n+1}=a_n+b_{n+1}$ together with an initial value.

questions.prompt: You are developing a sensor system. How many different values can a 12-bit field represent if every bit pattern is allowed?
questions.explanation: Each of the 12 bits has two possibilities. Therefore, there are $2^{12}=4096$ different bit patterns, and hence 4096 values.

questions.prompt: A compiler checks a loop: an invariant holds before the first iteration, and each iteration preserves it. What is the mathematical core of this check?

options.text: Gray code
L-tromino tiling
An induction proof with a base case and an induction step
Prime factorization

questions.explanation: The induction base shows that the invariant holds before the first iteration. The induction step shows that each subsequent iteration preserves its validity.

questions.prompt: A computer algebra system first factors $60$ into $6\cdot10$, and then continues processing $6$ and $10$. Why is strong induction appropriate here?

options.text: All intermediate results are added together.
The subproblems may be any smaller numbers, not just $n-1$.
The board is divided into four quadrants.
Each new state must differ in exactly one bit.

questions.explanation: Prime factorization creates subproblems involving different smaller numbers. Strong induction can therefore use all already-proved cases for smaller numbers.

questions.prompt: In the puzzle game, you have a $32\times32$ board with exactly one missing square. How many L-trominoes do you need to tile it completely?
questions.explanation: The board has $32^2-1=1023$ squares to cover. Since each L-tromino covers three squares, $1023/3=341$ L-trominoes are needed. Equivalently, $(4^5-1)/3=341$.

questions.prompt: There are 13 people in your tutorial group. Which statement is guaranteed without any additional information?

options.text: Exactly one month contains two birthdays.
At least two people have birthdays on the same calendar day.
At least two people have birthdays in the same month.
At least one person has a birthday in every month.

questions.explanation: There are 13 people but only 12 birth months. By the pigeonhole principle, at least two people must therefore have birthdays in the same month.

questions.prompt: You are logging an LED display whose values increase as follows: $1,2,4,\dots,2^{10}$. What is the sum of all the logged values?
questions.explanation: This is the geometric sum $\sum_{k=0}^{10}2^k=2^{11}-1=2047$.

questions.prompt: You are programming a puzzle game: a $2^n\times2^n$ board has one blocked square. Your algorithm divides it into four quadrants, places an L at the center, and calls itself again on the smaller boards. Which idea from the unit is being implemented directly?

options.text: Prime factorization
Recursive tiling with L-trominoes
Geometric sum
Gray code for sensor signals

questions.explanation: This is the recursive construction in Golomb's theorem: a central L-tromino creates one virtually missing square in each of the three quadrants without a blocked square. The smaller boards are then tiled recursively.

questions.prompt: An app's local counter starts at $0$ and assigns the next number to each new order: $0,1,2,\dots$. Which idea from the unit models this mechanism?

options.text: Gray code
L-tromino tiling
Prime factorization
Successor function $S(n)=n+1$

questions.explanation: Each new number is the successor of the previous one. This corresponds to the successor function and the construction of the natural numbers starting from $0$.
